extracted.intended_audience: students, reformers, and policymakers assessing the applicability of representative government; readers of political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether representative government is appropriate or likely to succeed in a given society by applying social, moral, and institutional criteria (citizen capacity, public opinion, social cohesion, stage of civilization, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental conditions for permanence of representative government
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government can permanently subsist only if three fundamental conditions are met: (1) the people should be willing to receive it; (2) they should be willing and able to do what is necessary for its preservation; (3) they should be willing and able to fulfill the duties and discharge the functions which it imposes on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three conditions are the baseline test: absence of any makes representative government unsuitable. The text emphasizes that without public willingness and capacity both to defend institutions and to discharge civic duties, representation will fail or be short-lived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective public opinion/backing to check the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative institutions require that bodies checking the executive be 'backed by an effective opinion and feeling in the country'; otherwise the executive can set aside or compel compliance from representative organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the populace does not value representative institutions enough to defend them, the executive will overpower or co-opt them. The permanence of representation depends on the people's readiness to 'fight for them' when endangered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen interest and capacity to form public opinion/use suffrage responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: A people must possess the will and capacity to form a public opinion and to use suffrage for the public good rather than merely private, local, or factional ends; otherwise representatives become place-hunters and public representation degenerates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only a small, self-interested fraction cares for general affairs, elections serve private/local interests and lead to corruption, instability, or assemblies that merely provide publicity without effective governance. Example: assemblies that are 'place-hunters' keep up forms of representation but not substantive public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active, self-helping national character
rubrics_metrics.description: A national character marked by activity, ambition, and self-help is suited to representative government because it fosters effort, public spirit, and the pursuit of improvements; passive or indulgent national character favors envy and indolence and is less suited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Anglo-Saxon energetic self-helping types (England, United States) with more envious/passive types (Orientals, some Southern Europeans). Active character both creates the desire and supplies the energy needed for meaningful civic participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of civic functions that educate citizens (participation as civic schooling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunities for ordinary citizens to perform public functions (jury service, parish offices, dicasteries, ecclesia) act as practical civic education, enlarging conceptions and sentiments and improving faculties necessary for representative government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book gives historical examples: Athenian dicasteries and ecclesia raised civic intellect; English jury and parish service improve the lower middle class. Even occasional public duties discipline citizens to 'weigh interests not their own' and foster identification with the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage of civilization / general improvement of the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government is more suitable to peoples with a sufficient degree of general improvement; in early or low stages of development it may be inapplicable or counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues the adaptation to representation depends on special requisites tied to overall advancement; very early-stage societies may need different regimes (e.g., central authority, despotism) to reach the prerequisites for representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for prior acquisition of obedience in certain societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a population still needs to learn the 'first lesson of civilization'—obedience—representative government can be an impediment; centralized or despotic authority (often through military leadership) may be necessary to instill order first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tributary or warlike tribes accustomed to turbulent insubordination will produce assemblies that reflect that turbulence; historical practice often used strong central rulers or military command to secure obedience before representative institutions could be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme passiveness/readiness to submit to tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: If a people is extremely passive and ready to submit, representative institutions will be used to select tyrants and will worsen the yoke rather than relieve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such societies, giving them representation can legitimize and entrench oppression because the populace will choose representatives who serve tyranny; in some cases central authority has been necessary to lift such peoples out of prostration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong spirit of locality / lack of nation-wide sympathies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where jealousies, antipathies, or parochial local attachments prevent amalgamation into a larger political unit, representative government is unlikely to succeed without a prior central authority to weld the political atoms into a people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical claim: numerous small political units usually coalesce into nations only after subjection to a central authority which creates common interests and habits of deference; representative bodies drawn from localities may be useful auxiliaries if they act with the central power rather than seeking to control it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social heterogeneity: presence of a markedly superior small class
rubrics_metrics.description: When a small leading portion of the population is markedly superior in civilization/character to the remainder, full popular representation can either deprive that minority of beneficial influence or, conversely, rule in a way that cements the degradation of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best prospects in such cases may lie with a strong chief ruler of the dominant class who has an interest in raising the mass, sometimes aided by a representative body of the superior ranks acting as a check and a seed for future national representation (example: English historical development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant political inclinations: appetite for governing others vs desire for personal independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative strength of two dispositions—(a) desire to exercise power over others, and (b) disinclination to have power exercised over oneself—affects suitability: populations driven by place-hunting and ambition for offices favor wide forms of representation but may produce overgovernment and corruption; populations jealous of being governed but indifferent to wielding power fit a limited representative model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where passion to govern others is strong, representative institutions may be sought chiefly to open offices to competition and produce excessive meddling; where people prefer to be free from others' power and disdain governing, they may accept rule by social superiors and still guard limits on overreach (the English tendency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial/nominal representative institutions can still yield benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when representation is imperfect or dominated by place-hunters, the existence of representative assemblies can preserve the idea of popular rights, maintain press liberty, and generate publicity and discussion that are of public value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: modern Greece—assemblies composed chiefly of place-hunters still contribute to the persistence of popular-rights discourse and to the real liberty of the press; such benefits, however, depend on other features (e.g., coexistence with an hereditary king) and are not a substitute for genuine representative functioning.
